sedition

sih-DISH-un · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Sedition is conduct or speech inciting people to rebel against the authority of a state or government.

The pamphlets calling for an armed uprising against the king were quickly seized and burned as sedition.

Example

The general was arrested and charged with sedition after secretly encouraging soldiers to turn against the government that commanded them.

Sedition specifically targets government authority -- it's a serious legal and political charge, not just any rebellious attitude.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

rebellion: Rebellion is open resistance or defiance against authority -- people actually rising up. Sedition comes one step earlier: it is the speech or conduct that stirs others toward that uprising. You can commit sedition with nothing but words, before a single act of defiance happens.

subversion: Subversion works in secret -- quiet efforts to weaken or overthrow a system from inside it. Sedition is usually loud and open: pamphlets, speeches, public calls to defy the government. A spy planted in a ministry commits subversion; a street orator urging revolt commits sedition.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

loyalty: faithful support and allegiance

conformity: behavior that follows accepted standards or rules

Where it sits · how serious a crime it becomes

dissent → sedition → treason

dissent vs. sedition: Dissent is open disagreement with an official policy -- lawful in most places and much milder than sedition, which crosses the line into urging revolt against the government itself.

treason vs. sedition: Treason is the crime of betraying one's country, especially by attempting to overthrow the government -- even more severe than sedition.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — sed-: apart, aside (Latin se-, taking the form sed- before a vowel -- the same piece that starts sequester and separate)

Root (not standalone) — -ition: a going -- not a standalone English word on its own (Latin itio, from ire, 'to go')

Put it together: Sedition comes from Latin seditio: sed- (the form of se-, 'apart,' used before a vowel) + -ition ('a going,' from itio, from ire 'to go') -- literally 'a going apart.' It names speech or action meant to make people break away from lawful authority.

Use the root in a new word: sequester: The jury was sequestered before the lawyers had even finished their closing arguments.

Word Building

Word Choice

Sedition is a serious legal and political term -- it describes speech or action that incites rebellion against a government, and it shows up most often in news, history, and law rather than everyday conversation.
